claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by microstructural stability under mechanical stress.
The initial high-entropy-alloy coatings have a homogeneous microstructure.
Cyclic mechanical loading simulates wear conditions.
Mechanical loading can produce phase transformations in the coatings.
Mechanical loading can produce dislocation movement in the coatings.
Mechanical loading can produce grain-boundary sliding in the coatings.
The coating microstructure evolves under mechanical stress.
Stress-induced microstructural evolution affects coating hardness.
Stress-induced microstructural evolution affects wear resistance.
A stable microstructure leads to better wear performance.
Under the same loading conditions, coatings with more stable microstructures will have lower wear rates than coatings with less stable microstructures.
The proposed relationship should hold for high-entropy alloys with similar compositions and processing methods.
The proposed relationship may not hold for alloys with significantly different microstructural characteristics.
The relationship between microstructural stability and wear performance may depend on alloy composition and environmental conditions.
The designated baseline is coating wear performance without applied mechanical loading.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as having no applied mechanical loading, whereas the predicted and falsifying comparisons require coatings with different microstructural stabilities to be tested under the same or identical loading. Thus, the stated baseline does not isolate microstructural stability and may not constitute a wear test unless 'mechanical loading' means an additional load beyond wear contact.
